insights.topic: Unsafe type assertions (as any) in production code bypass type safety and mask runtime shape mismatches
insights.suggestion: Replace `as any` with strict type guards or Zod schema validation at API boundaries. The two remaining `as any` casts in binance.ts (exchangeInfo, depth) and the `(config as any).webhooks` in webhook.ts are the last line-prod holes after the indicators.ts MACD fix.
insights.evidence: src/binance.ts:187 (`return (await res.json()) as any;` in fetchExchangeInfo), src/binance.ts:202 (`return (await res.json()) as any;` in fetchDepth), src/core/webhook.ts:36 (`(config as any).webhooks as WebhookConfig | undefined`). These are tracked as P0 (t_112b666a) and P1 (t_cddfeb6b) blocked on dev in the kanban.

insights.topic: API bearer token comparison uses non-constant-time operator, enabling timing side-channel attacks
insights.suggestion: Replace `!==` with `crypto.timingSafeEqual()` for the apiToken comparison. An attacker on the same network (or localhost) could iteratively guess the token by measuring response latency differences.
insights.evidence: src/api/rest.ts:36 (`if (!config.apiToken || token !== config.apiToken)`) — the Bearer token extracted from Authorization header is compared with a simple strict inequality. Node.js provides `crypto.timingSafeEqual` in the standard library for this exact purpose.

insights.topic: Telegram bot token is embedded in fetch URL path; Node.js error messages can leak the full URL to logs
insights.suggestion: Strip query parameters and mask the bot token in log/error output. Consider passing the token in a header instead of the URL path, or implement a dedicated fetch wrapper that redacts the token portion before logging errors.
insights.evidence: src/core/webhook.ts:73 (`const url = \`https://api.telegram.org/bot${botToken}/sendMessage\``). If the Telegram API fetch fails, the Node.js `fetch` error message includes the full URL by default, which would surface the botToken in warn-level logs (line 86: `log.warn(\`Telegram API returned ${response.status}\`)`).

insights.topic: Daemon mutating HTTP endpoints (/reload-config, /refresh, /scan-complete) have no authentication at all
insights.suggestion: Add at minimum the same Bearer token check used in POST /api/collect to all mutating daemon routes. The warm-daemon's /refresh endpoint (warm-daemon.ts) also lacks auth. While bound to 127.0.0.1, local processes including compromised containers could abuse these.
insights.evidence: src/daemon.ts:165-174 (/refresh), 177-187 (/reload-config), 190-196 (/scan-complete POST) — none of these routes validate the apiToken. src/core/warm-daemon.ts:110-127 (/refresh) also has no auth. Only POST /api/collect in src/api/rest.ts:31-41 has bearer auth.

insights.topic: Daemon HTTP server lacks rate limiting — /refresh and /reload-config can be hammered without throttle
insights.suggestion: Apply the existing RateLimiter class (already used for Binance API calls) to incoming HTTP requests. Without rate limiting, a local attacker or misbehaving Hermes agent can trigger rapid cache refreshes, starving the Node process.
insights.evidence: src/daemon.ts imports no RateLimiter for HTTP requests; the RateLimiter class at src/core/rate-limiter.ts is only used for outbound API calls in src/sources/orderbook.ts and src/sources/futures.ts. The config at src/core/config.ts:89-90 defines rateLimitMax=20 and rateLimitWindowMs=1000 but these are never applied to daemon HTTP routes.

insights.topic: Config singleton (loadConfig) caches apiToken indefinitely — stale token persists after env var change
insights.suggestion: Re-read the apiToken from process.env on each authenticated request instead of caching it in the singleton. Or invalidate _instance when RADAR__API_TOKEN changes. Currently the token is frozen at first loadConfig() call for the process lifetime.
insights.evidence: src/core/config.ts:117 (`let _instance: RadarConfig | null = null;`), line 127-128 (`if (_instance) return _instance;`), line 195 (`if (envMap.api_token) base.apiToken = envMap.api_token;`). The singleton caches the entire config including apiToken on first load, ignoring subsequent env changes.

insights.topic: RADAR__WEBHOOK_URL in .env.example suggests credential-in-env pattern but is not actually wired, creating config confusion risk
insights.suggestion: Either wire the env var into the webhook config path, or remove it from .env.example to prevent users from falsely believing their webhook secret is being picked up. The actual webhook config lives in radar.config.json, not env vars.
insights.evidence: .env.example:73 (`# RADAR__WEBHOOK_URL=`) shows a commented env var for webhook URLs. Code search confirms no `process.env` read for `WEBHOOK_URL` or `webhook_url` in any .ts file — the webhook values are loaded from radar.config.json via the webhooks config block (src/core/config.ts:75-81).

insights.topic: Webhook test file uses `as any` to mock config, mirroring production's type-unsafe pattern
insights.suggestion: Use typed mock factories (e.g., `vi.mocked(loadConfig).mockReturnValue(...)`) with explicit partial types instead of casting mock objects to `any`. This pattern in tests normalizes the unsafe pattern that then appears in production.
insights.evidence: src/core/webhook.test.ts:79 (`} as any);`) — the test suite uses `as any` to bypass type checking on the mock return value of `loadConfig`. While only a test concern, it reinforces the same unsafe type-erasure anti-pattern present in production webhook.ts:36.
